2005.history: The hill in the north-west where a pit was worked for the only good flint on Dia-thìr, its grey flakes carried to hearths from one end of the island to the other. The carriers' track ran from the pit-mouth south and east toward Cruinneachadh an Àtha, and by the thousand eight hundred and seventeenth year it was worn a yard deep. Murchadh, the king's son by Beitris, came here with the flint-carriers in the thousand seven hundred and sixtieth year and carried a yoke for three seasons before any man learned whose son he was; he walked the road with Ailig Spor for the whole of the years it gave them, and when Ailig took the lighter work of tallying at the pit-mouth Murchadh came back through at the turn of every season to sit an evening with him. After Ailig's burying Murchadh set it as a standing custom that the first flake of any new working be given free to whoever asked.
2005.known_for: the flint-pit and the free first flake

436.history: A great ford of the north on the far eastern circuit of Rathad na Spor. In the thousand eight hundred and fifty-third year a young man of the ford cut a hawk into his father's door-lintel by firelight over three evenings, wings closed and the head turned back over the shoulder; he said only that the shape had come to him whole one night and would not leave him alone until he had cut it. Murchadh watched him cut it. It is the oldest carving of a hawk on the island, and of any bird, and the lintel was set again over every door the household built after.

435.history: A wild spring on the moor whose herders walked the same paths through the whole of the age, and whose spring was said never to fail. The households of the spring buried wolves whole and with care, laid on their sides with their legs drawn up as in sleep, a care they spoke of to no one outside the household; an old woman told Murchadh, who came on a burying in the thousand eight hundred and ninetieth year, that the wolf kept its own dead on the high ground and had earned better than the ditch. No other beast was so buried in the age.

22.history: A broad headland on the gulf where, in the two thousand and seventy-sixth year, three brothers of the point, Aonghas, Dùghlas and Ailig mac Torcaill, quarried eight stones from an outcrop above the landing and raised them in a ring, one for each of the named winds, so a sailor might lay a hand on the stone of the wind he wanted before he put out. The stone of the hardest offshore wind settled crooked in a bad winter and was dug out and reset on a footing of smaller stones, standing straighter and newer than its seven fellows ever after. The yearly contests of strength were held below Clachan nan Gaoth, and it was here that Alasdair Làidir threw every man at three-and-twenty and a grey stranger lifted the black boulder to his knees and set it down gently.
22.known_for: Clachan nan Gaoth and the lifted boulder

2003.history: A black hill in the east where Torcall Tochlair, refused the marriage he was promised and restless at the coal-banks under the mountain, went with his brother Lachann and two other diggers to open a trench for a second vein. In the two thousand two hundred and sixty-seventh year the trench fell in on two of them, Lachann among them, and Torcall buried his brother at the trench's mouth and would not leave. He built a turf shelter at the trench's edge, and folk who came to the hill for one reason or another began to stay, since the ground was as good as any and the man who kept the trench asked nothing of them. He died there and was buried beside his brother. His household kept the ground, did not fill the trench in, and in Catrìona's years refused to burn its handful of coal with the rest of the hills, giving no single answer twice for it.
2003.known_for: the open trench and the refused handful

166.history: A harbour of the south-west where, in the two thousand four hundred and twenty-fourth year, households hearing only that the Ros dhomhain keeper cut her marks at a certain interval began cutting their own high-water marks on the harbour rock at that same spacing, though none of them could say why that width and no other. So three tide-rocks were kept side by side on the island, and the interval travelled without its reasoning.
